description: References behind data/traditions/*.json. Every fact in this lane is a paraphrase written for ALEF; no sentences were copied. 'fetched' is the date a page was read in this build session (an AI agent read the text through a fetch tool). 'coverage' says how much of the page was read, because some pages were long.
licenceNote: Wikipedia article text is CC BY-SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/). We copy no wording, only facts, and cite each page. If you treat the paraphrased notes in sounds.json as adaptations, they are offered under the same CC BY-SA 4.0 licence with attribution to the pages listed here; that is a precaution, not a legal opinion. Pealim, Chabad.org and the BJPA paper are NOT openly licensed: they are cited by URL only, as references a reader can open.

sources.title: Sephardi Hebrew (Wikipedia)
sources.coverage: whole page summarised by the fetch tool
sources.supports: pharyngeal ayin and het among several Sephardi communities; Western Sephardim use a nasal for ayin; alveolar r; tav as t in standard Sephardi and Israeli, th in Greek and some Mizrahi groups; popular speech does not separate patah and kamatz gadol; tsere and holam are plain e and o; shva na read as e; Israeli Hebrew dropped the pharyngeals and shifted resh

sources.title: Ashkenazi Hebrew (Wikipedia)
sources.coverage: whole page summarised by the fetch tool
sources.supports: unaccented tav as s; kamatz gadol as a back rounded vowel (o or aw), u in southern dialects; cholam and tsere regional values; traditional penultimate stress with final stress promoted for Torah reading; ayin, het and alef silent in most forms; resh varies by dialect; Israeli Hebrew was meant to follow Sephardi values but absorbed some Ashkenazi features; Yemenite keeps kamatz and patah apart but not patah and segol

sources.title: Modern Hebrew phonology (Wikipedia)
sources.coverage: whole page summarised by the fetch tool
sources.supports: older Oriental (Mizrahi) speakers often keep pharyngeal het and, less commonly, ayin; general Israeli ayin merged into the glottal stop; het merged with khaf for most; qof merged into k; resh uvular for nearly all Israeli Jews, alveolar trill often kept by immigrants from Arabic-speaking countries; five-vowel system with no audible length contrast; stress final or penultimate and now meaning-bearing; Standard Israeli based on Sephardi Hebrew

sources.title: Yemenite Hebrew (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: pharyngeal het and ayin; gimel without dagesh as a voiced throat fricative and with dagesh as j; tav raphe as th; dalet raphe as dh; patah and segol sound alike; penultimate stress claim is tagged 'citation needed' on the page, so ALEF does not rely on it

sources.title: Pronunciations of Hebrew (Pealim.com article)
sources.licence: not openly licensed; cited by URL, facts paraphrased
sources.coverage: whole page summarised by the fetch tool; page does not discuss ayin
sources.supports: tav t versus s; kamatz, cholam, tsere values in Ashkenazi versus Sephardi/Israeli; Ashkenazi stress usually penultimate except in public religious readings; het versus khaf and qof versus kaf still distinct in some Mizrahi or Georgian liturgical traditions; traditional pronunciations survive mainly in synagogues and religious schools

sources.title: The Difference Between Sepharadic and Ashkenazic Pronunciation (Chabad.org)
sources.licence: not openly licensed; cited by URL, facts paraphrased
sources.coverage: whole page summarised by the fetch tool; page does not discuss stress
sources.supports: unaccented tav; kamatz versus patach; cholam; tsere and segol; Sephardim distinguish alef/ayin and het/khaf, Ashkenazim generally do not; many variants inside each grouping; modern Hebrew read with 'Sepharadic' values by many Jews of both backgrounds; the page says all dialects are acceptable

sources.title: Survey of Jewish English and Hebrew usage, popular paper (Benor and Cohen, via BJPA)
sources.licence: not openly licensed; cited by URL, facts paraphrased
sources.coverage: whole PDF summarised by the fetch tool
sources.supports: for the single word 'Festival of Booths', Reform, Reconstructionist and Conservative respondents more often chose the Israeli form while Orthodox and Black Hat respondents more often chose the Ashkenazic form; self-reported, snowball sample, not representative of all American Jews, one or two example words only; many people use both forms depending on audience
